title: Strategy Leadership Lab
text:
Content Overview
Strategy Leadership Lab is a weekly working session for the roughly 30 students who lead the BYU Strategy Program and the four career clubs it administers: MCA, PMA, CSA, and WSA. Those clubs serve students across campus by career interest rather than by major, and the leadership team reflects that: about half of the people in this room are majoring in something other than strategy. It exists to do two things at once: develop you as a leader, and give the whole leadership team protected time to coordinate on shared priorities.
The Lab is the primary coordination mechanism in the Strategy Program operating model. One meeting cadence governs the entire program.
Enrollment is limited to program and club leaders and is open to them regardless of major. It is optional but encouraged for everyone serving in a presidency. If your schedule prevents you from enrolling, you are welcome to audit or simply attend.

Credit and Pay
Students do not receive pay and credit for the same work.

Class is where you reflect, discuss, and learn. The job is where you execute, deliver, and coordinate.
Student employees may not log paid work hours during scheduled class sessions or on class-specific assignments.

title: Operating Model
text:
Strategy Program Operating Model
The Strategy Program administers four career clubs that serve students across campus. Club membership is open by career interest, not by major: a student headed for consulting, product, or corporate strategy belongs in the relevant club whether they are a strategy major or not. Roughly half the leaders in this room are majoring in something else.
The program has grown by 50% over the last five years and now serves 120 new students per year through the major, and the clubs reach a wider group than that. The operating model below aligns faculty, student leaders, career services, and academic advisement at that scale. It has three parts.

2. The Clubs
Each career club exists to open doors and prepare students for a specific profession. The clubs are organized around where students are headed, not what they are majoring in, and are open to students from any major. title: Session Template
text:
Session Template
Every session runs the same five blocks in the same order, the way a practice does. The sequence does not change week to week. What changes is the content inside each block.
The first four blocks are the 30 minute leadership development block. Practice is the 45 minute working block, published on the schedule as the project roundtable.

title: Session Template
text:
Announcements (5 min)
Program logistics only. Anything that takes longer than a minute to explain belongs in Practice or in email. Standing items:

Upcoming club events and who owns them
Deadlines landing this week or next
Recruiting calendar changes
New hires, role changes, vacancies

title: Session Template
section: Quote of the Day and Leader Profile (5 min)
text:
Quote of the Day and Leader Profile (5 min)
One quote and one leader, together in five minutes. Keep the profile to three or four sentences: who they are, the decision or moment worth knowing, what it cost them.
Rotate who presents. A student leader takes this block, signs up a week ahead, and picks both the quote and the profile. The only constraint is that the pair should connect to the week’s principle.

title: Session Template
text:
Leadership Principle (10 min)
One principle, taught. The operating model names three skill areas to draw from: influence, conflict, and managing up. Guest speakers and case discussions fill this block too.
Ten minutes buys one idea, not three. State the principle, give one example of it working, give one example of it failing, then move to Drills.

title: Session Template
text:
Drills (10 min)
A follow-along. You are at the front with your screen up, everyone has a laptop open, and the room builds the same thing at the same time. Nobody watches a demo. If a student’s screen is dark, the drill is not working.
The default format is an AI follow-along: you narrate the prompt, everyone types their own version, and the interesting part is where the outputs differ. Ten minutes is enough for one artifact, not a workflow. Pick something a leader would actually produce this week.
Candidates:

Draft the recruiting email to a firm contact, then compare what six people got back
Turn a messy set of event notes into a one page brief
Build the agenda for a club presidency meeting from a two sentence description
Take a plan someone wrote and have AI argue against it, then judge whether it was right
Summarize a case or article into the three sentences you would say out loud

Rules that keep it a drill and not a lecture:

Everyone types. You go slow enough that the slowest person keeps up.
Same starting prompt for the room, so the differences are visible.
Stop at ten minutes even if it is unfinished. Unfinished is fine, it makes the point.
Two or three people read their output out loud before you move on.

If a follow-along needs more room, take the extra five minutes from Practice rather than from the Principle block.

title: Session Template
text:
Practice (45 min)
Students take the rest of the hour and actually do the work. The drill showed them the move once. Practice is where they run it on their own club’s real deliverable, at their own desk, for forty five minutes.
Scott, Sarah, and Luke roam the room the whole time. Roaming is the instruction method here. There is no front of the room during Practice.
What roaming looks like:

Read over a shoulder before saying anything
Ask what they are trying to do, not what they are doing
Two minutes per student, then move. Come back around rather than camping.
Carry patterns forward: if three people hit the same wall, stop the room and say so

Sarah and Luke have two modes and can pick per week:

In the room. Roam alongside Scott, same job, three coaches covering thirty students.
Broken out. Pull a subgroup into a side conversation: a club that needs focused help, a first-time VP who needs onboarding, a team with a deadline that week. Or run their own work while available to the room.

Decide the mode in prep, not on the fly, so the room knows who to look for.
Club and presidency updates and cross-team coordination still need a home. Either give them the first ten minutes of Practice before students scatter, or fold the standing items into Announcements. Pick one and keep it the same every week.

title: Session Template
text:
Weekly Prep Checklist

Announcements collected from club leaders by Thursday
Quote and Leader Profile presenter confirmed
Principle chosen, with one success example and one failure example
Follow-along built and run once yourself, with the starting prompt written down
Practice: what each club is working on, so roaming has a target
Sarah and Luke’s mode set for the week: roaming or broken out
